data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is not primarily a thermal storage or anthropogenic heat phenomenon but a radiative shielding effect: the urban canopy blocks a fraction of the sky, reducing radiative cooling to space. The single best cross-city modulator is sky view factor: cities with lower average sky view factor have slower nocturnal cooling rates and thus larger nocturnal UHI gaps, independent of thermal mass or anthropogenic heat.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If thermal storage release is shown to dominate over radiative shielding in nocturnal UHI formation","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If sky view factor alone cannot predict cross-city variation without including thermal mass or anthropogenic heat","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI is absent or very small in cities with low sky view factor but low thermal mass","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If wind speed rather than radiative geometry is the dominant control on nocturnal cooling","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"On a clear calm night, the dominant cooling mechanism is longwave radiative loss to the sky. The urban canopy, through building geometry, reduces the effective sky view factor, so urban surfaces radiate to warmer building walls rather than to cold sky. This radiative shielding slows the urban cooling rate. The countryside has an unobstructed view to the sky and cools rapidly. Cities with lower sky view factor have more suppressed radiative cooling and thus a larger nocturnal UHI gap. This mechanism is independent of thermal mass and anthropogenic heat, which are secondary.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
